title: Formalized, the major is false: a first principle need not prove itself or be evident
source_text: IV. Ut autem hujus argumenti fraus et vitium detegatur, ad formam revocandum est. Sic igitur necesse est ut illi argumententur. Quod ex se non est evidens, nec seipsum probare potest, illud non est primum fidei principium, et suprema fidei regula, cujus authoritas aliunde non pendet, sed ipsum per aliud probari necesse est. At Scriptura non est aliquid evidens, nec seipsam probare potest. Ergo, &c. Jam vero major hujus argumenti est falsi manifesta. Nam plane contra necesse est, ut quod est primum fidei principium, neque seipsum probet, nec per aliud probetur; nec tamen sit aliquid evidens. Etenim quemadmodum in disciplinis humanis quaedam sunt prima principia, unde reliqua pendent, et per quae caetera probantur, ipsa tamen neque a se, neque ab aliis in hoc genere pendent, alioqui prima non essent, sed per se fidem et assensum obtinent: ita quoque res se habet in fidei doctrina. Vel enim debet hic admitti circulus, aut dari progressus in infinitum, quorum utrumque est absurdum; aut necessario sistendum est in principio aliquo, unde pendeant, et per quod probentur caetera quae ad fidem pertinent, ipsum tamen a nullo priori, scilicet, probetur, neque etiam a seipso: quandoquidem idem non potest a seipso probari: sed per se fidem et assensum obtineat, et cui immediate credamus et assentiamur.
pass_a_gloss: But in order that the fraud and fault of this argument may be uncovered, it must be reduced to form. Thus therefore it is necessary that they argue: That which is not evident of itself, and cannot prove itself, is not a first principle of faith and supreme rule of faith whose authority does not depend from elsewhere, but it is necessary that it itself be proved through another. But Scripture is not something evident, nor can it prove itself. Therefore, etc. Now in truth the major of this argument is of manifest falsity. For plainly on the contrary it is necessary that what is a first principle of faith neither prove itself nor be proved through another; and yet that it not be something evident. For just as in human disciplines there are certain first principles from which the rest depend and through which the others are proved, yet they themselves depend neither from themselves nor from others in this kind, otherwise they would not be first, but obtain faith and assent through themselves: so also the matter stands in the doctrine of faith. For either a circle must be admitted here, or a progress to infinity given, both of which are absurd; or necessarily a stand must be made in some principle from which the rest that pertain to faith depend and through which they are proved, yet it itself is proved by no prior principle, namely, nor even by itself: since the same thing cannot be proved by itself: but let it obtain faith and assent through itself, and to it let us immediately believe and assent.
pass_b_english: To expose the cheat, reduce the argument to form. They must argue: whatever is not evident of itself and cannot prove itself is not a first principle of faith or supreme rule whose authority does not hang elsewhere — it must be proved through something else. But Scripture is not evident, nor can it prove itself. Therefore, and so on.

The major is plainly false. On the contrary: what is a first principle of faith must neither prove itself nor be proved through another — and yet need not be something evident. In the human sciences some principles are first: the rest hang on them and are proved through them, while they hang on nothing else in that order, or they would not be first, and win assent of themselves. Faith is the same.

Either admit a circle, or an infinite regress — both absurd — or stop at some principle on which the rest of faith hangs, proved by no prior principle and not by itself either, since the same thing cannot prove itself, yet winning immediate belief and assent of itself.

lemmas.gloss: to be reduced to syllogistic form
